I am 67 years old, and I have walked these fields in Quzhou County for 45 years. My wife and I make up the household now—our children work in the city and send money home, but they cannot help at planting or harvest. With only two of us and 16.1 mu of land, I must be careful with labor. The wheat-maize double cropping system is the backbone of our farm because it is highly mechanized and gives us two harvests per year from the same soil. I know the window between wheat harvest and maize sowing in June is tight—only a few days—so I have learned to plant maize with no-tillage directly into the wheat stubble. It saves diesel, time, and precious soil moisture. I keep about 5 mu of cotton because the price per jin is much better than grain, but I will not expand it; cotton requires hand labor for topping and near-weekly spraying against bollworm, and at my age I cannot manage more than that. I have a well for irrigation, so drought is not my biggest fear, but electricity costs money, so I irrigate three times for wheat and twice each for maize and cotton—enough to keep yields steady without wasting water. My education means I can read fertilizer recommendations and pesticide labels, and over the decades I have learned that a basal compound fertilizer followed by a top-dressing of urea at jointing gives the wheat what it needs. For seed, I buy improved wheat varieties like the ones I have trusted for years, hybrid maize for vigor, and improved cotton seed for the local climate. I expect wheat around 1,050 jin per mu, maize around 1,100 jin per mu, and cotton around 550 jin per mu—honest yields for honest work on this land.
